items.topic: Facility fire extinguisher — PASS: Pull, Aim at base, Squeeze, Sweep
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A small wastebasket fire starts in an unoccupied utility room. After activating the alarm and confirming a clear exit path, the nurse uses a portable extinguisher. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep side to side
Aim at the top of the flames, then pull the pin and squeeze once briefly
Spray water from a pitcher first, then store the extinguisher unused
Squeeze the handle continuously while aiming only at smoke near the ceiling

rationales.A: Correct. OSHA and nursing references teach the PASS technique: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep side to side at the base until the fire appears out.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Aiming at the top of the flames misses the fuel source at the base; pin is pulled first.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Improvised water is not the extinguisher PASS technique and may be unsafe for some fire types.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Aiming at ceiling smoke does not extinguish the fire at its base.

items.topic: Vancomycin IV — flushing syndrome from rapid infusion; infuse over ≥60 minutes
items.stem: During the first minutes of an IV vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and pruritus of the face and neck without wheezing or hypotension. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Slow or temporarily stop the infusion and resume at a slower rate over at least 60 minutes as ordered/protocol
Double the remaining dose into a rapid IV push to finish sooner
Immediately give a monoamine oxidase inhibitor to reverse flushing
Ignore the flushing because vancomycin never causes infusion reactions

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: vancomycin flushing syndrome from too-rapid IV administration is managed by slowing the infusion and giving each dose over at least 60 minutes. Merck: infuse slowly over ≥60 minutes to avoid histamine-mediated infusion reaction with facial/neck flushing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Faster administration worsens the reaction; IV push is inappropriate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. MAOIs are unrelated and unsafe here.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Rapid infusion is a recognized cause of vancomycin infusion/flushing reaction.

items.topic: NGN cloze — vancomycin infusion duration and flushing-reaction management
items.stem: Complete the safe-administration teaching for IV vancomycin.

ngn.template: Each IV vancomycin dose should be infused over at least {B1}. If vancomycin flushing syndrome occurs from a rapid infusion, the usual first management step is to {B2}.

B1.text: 30 seconds as an undiluted IV push

B2.text: slow the infusion (and follow protocol/provider orders)
give the next dose twice as fast
add an MAOI to the same IV line
stop all future antibiotics permanently without assessment

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: infuse each dose over at least 60 minutes.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. IV push of vancomycin is unsafe and promotes flushing reaction.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Five minutes is too rapid for typical vancomycin doses.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Continuous 24-hour infusion is not the standard teaching for each intermittent dose duration.
rationales.B2a: Correct. OpenStax: management is to slow the infusion; flushing syndrome can be mistaken for allergy.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Faster infusion worsens histamine release.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. MAOI coadministration is unrelated and dangerous.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Assessment and protocol-guided management are required; automatic permanent stop without evaluation is incorrect teaching.

items.topic: Vesicant chemotherapy extravasation — stop infusion immediately; follow protocol
items.stem: While a vesicant chemotherapy infusion is running, the client reports burning at the peripheral IV site and the nurse notes swelling. What is the immediate priority action?

options.text: Stop the infusion immediately and follow the facility extravasation protocol (including provider notification)
Increase the infusion rate to finish the dose before tissue contact continues
Flush the line vigorously with a large fluid bolus and ignore the burning
Leave the room for 30 minutes to see if the burning resolves on its own

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Pharmacology: if the IV site may be compromised during vesicant administration, stop the infusion immediately, notify the provider, and follow applicable extravasation protocols. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: for extravasation, stop the infusion and follow agency-specific management (including aspiration steps per policy).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Faster infusion increases tissue exposure to the vesicant.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Flushing into compromised tissue can worsen extravasation injury; do not ignore burning.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Delay allows ongoing tissue injury; extravasation is an emergency.

items.topic: Fifth disease (parvovirus B19) — usually return to school after slapped-cheek rash appears
items.stem: A school-age child develops the bright "slapped cheek" rash of fifth disease (parvovirus B19) after a few days of mild cold symptoms and is now afebrile. Which teaching is most accurate about contagiousness and school attendance?

options.text: The child is usually unlikely to be contagious after the rash appears and can typically return to school if otherwise well and facility policy allows
The child must remain home for exactly 30 days after the rash fades
The rash means the child is most contagious and must be isolated in a negative-pressure room at school
Fifth disease spreads only from dogs and cats, so school contacts are irrelevant

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: people are most contagious early; unlikely contagious after later symptoms such as rash; usually safe to return to school after the rash appears. VDH school chart: once the characteristic rash appears, the child is not likely contagious and can return; exclusion not otherwise indicated beyond facility fever/rash policies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A fixed 30-day post-rash exclusion is not the standard guidance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contagiousness is highest before the rash, not after; negative-pressure school isolation is not indicated for typical fifth disease.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Human parvovirus B19 spreads person to person (respiratory/blood); pet parvoviruses are different.

items.topic: Child severe FBAO — cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts
items.stem: A responsive 4-year-old is choking, cannot speak or cough effectively, and is becoming cyanotic. Which intervention sequence is recommended while emergency help is activated?

options.text: Repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive
Blind finger sweeps of the throat before any other action
Abdominal thrusts only, never back blows, and only after the child becomes unresponsive
Infant-style chest thrusts alone without back blows, because abdominal thrusts are preferred in infants

rationales.A: Correct. 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS: for children with severe FBAO, use repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive. Merck supports abdominal thrusts for older/conscious children and distinguishes infant technique.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Blind finger sweeps are not recommended and may push the object deeper.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Current child guidance includes back blows alternating with abdominal thrusts while the child is still responsive with severe obstruction.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Infant technique uses back blows and chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are not used in infants. This client is a child, not an infant.

sources.publisher: American Heart Association / American Academy of Pediatrics

sources.evidence: For children with severe FBAO: repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts until object expelled or child unresponsive. Abdominal thrusts not for infants.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — child severe FBAO: back blows + abdominal thrusts; monitor airway
items.stem: A responsive preschooler suddenly cannot speak, has a weak cough, and shows cyanosis while eating. Complete the bowtie: the priority condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Severe foreign-body airway obstruction (choking) in a child
Mild seasonal allergies with easy speech and strong cough
Uncomplicated otitis media without airway compromise

actions.text: Activate emergency response and begin cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts
Continue cycles until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive (then start CPR)
Perform repeated blind finger sweeps before any back blows
Offer a large glass of water and leave the child alone to "cough it out" unsupervised
Start abdominal thrusts on an infant under 1 year as the first-line infant method

parameters.text: Ability to speak/cough and presence of cyanosis or unresponsiveness
Whether the foreign body is expelled and airway/breathing improve

rationales.K1: Correct. Inability to speak, weak cough, and cyanosis indicate severe FBAO.
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Mild allergies with strong cough are not severe obstruction.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Otitis media is unrelated to acute airway obstruction.
rationales.A1: Correct. Activate help and use 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts for a child.
rationales.A2: Correct. Continue until expulsion or unresponsiveness; then CPR.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Blind finger sweeps are not recommended.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Severe obstruction needs immediate relief maneuvers, not unsupervised waiting.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts are not the infant method.
rationales.P1: Correct. Monitor airway signs and responsiveness.
rationales.P2: Correct. Monitor expulsion and breathing improvement.

items.topic: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — cola-colored urine, edema, hypertension after strep
items.stem: A school-age child had streptococcal pharyngitis about 10 days ago and now has periorbital edema, elevated blood pressure, and cola-colored urine. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Poststreptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
Immediate anaphylaxis to residual throat lozenges
Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis only
Simple dehydration with normal urine colour and no edema

rationales.A: Correct. Merck/CDC: PSGN/PIGN follows group A strep pharyngitis or skin infection after a latent period and presents with hematuria (often dark/cola-colored), edema, hypertension, and proteinuria.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Timing and renal findings do not indicate acute anaphylaxis.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not cause cola urine, edema, and hypertension after strep.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The described findings are not simple dehydration.

items.topic: NGN matrix — PSGN monitoring and supportive actions indicated vs not
items.stem: For a child with suspected poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after recent strep infection, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Monitor blood pressure closely for hypertension

rationales.R5: Not indicated. Dark/cola urine is a classic warning sign of glomerulonephritis, not something to ignore.

items.topic: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis — begin within 60 minutes before incision
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A client is scheduled for a clean-contaminated abdominal procedure. Which timing best reflects evidence-based surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis for a typical rapidly infused antibiotic (for example, a cephalosporin)?

options.text: Begin administration within 60 minutes before incision so tissue levels are present when the incision is made
Give the first prophylactic dose only after the incision is already closed
Start prophylaxis 24 hours before surgery and continue for 2 weeks automatically
Omit all antibiotics for every procedure regardless of guideline indications

rationales.A: Correct. SHEA 2022: begin antimicrobial prophylaxis within 1 hour before incision (2 hours allowed for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones due to longer infusion). CDC 2017: time agents so bactericidal concentrations are established when the incision is made.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prophylaxis should be present at incision; postoperative-only first dose misses the goal of tissue levels at incision.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Prolonged automatic courses are not the standard prophylaxis approach and increase harm/resistance risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Prophylaxis is indicated for many procedures per guidelines.

sources.title: Strategies to prevent surgical site infections in acute-care hospitals: 2022 Update
sources.publisher: SHEA / IDSA / APIC (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol)
sources.section: Essential practices — antimicrobial prophylaxis timing
sources.evidence: Begin antimicrobial prophylaxis within 1 hour prior to incision; 2 hours allowed for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones; discontinue after closure.

sources.title: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Guideline for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection, 2017
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.section: Parenteral Antimicrobial Prophylaxis 1A.1 / 1E
sources.evidence: Time prophylaxis so bactericidal concentration is present when incision is made; do not give additional prophylactic doses after incision closed in clean/clean-contaminated cases.
